prompt:
Reddit post, r/houseplants.
Title: Husband brought home this beauty from a clean out. So naturally, I’m here  looking for any advice I can get on how to revive and possibly ID. So far all I’m getting is dracaena or ponytail palm? Please help me give her the best life!

So far I’ve cleaned out all the dead leaves and bark that was hanging loose (first pic). The soil is VERY dry and sandy. Do these require sandy soil? I’m planning on repotting once she acclimated please let me know which size is best. She had a grow light in a basement room without any real natural light.. should I keep using it? I have lots of natural light in south facing windows here in zone 5a.

Pot and all it weighs 25lbs.

On average daytime temps 76° and night is 52°

What is wrong with my plant?
answer:
**Most likely cause: a corn plant (*Dracaena fragrans*) with dry air and tap-water minerals browning its leaf tips.** The crispy brown tips and the dry soil fit that. Dry winter air is the other likely driver, since leaves can turn brown at the tips if indoor humidity is too low, and a humidifier may help, especially in winter when the house is heated. Fluoride is the more common cause, because brown, crispy leaf tips are almost always caused by fluoride in tap water or a buildup of fertilizer salts.

**The trunk is the real question.** Peeling bark can mean rot or just a dead side. Squeeze the cane just above the soil. Firm means it is probably fine. Loose, papery bark or a soft base means rot. Dracaenas quite often die on one side of the stem and continue to grow on the healthy side. Also, yellowing, dropping lower leaves are a normal part of the plant's aging process, so the bottom leaves are probably not a concern.

**Fixes, in order:**
1. **Check the trunk and roots.** If the cane is firm, just peel off the loose dead bark. If it is soft or the roots are black and mushy, unpot it and cut away the rot before repotting.
2. **Water by the soil, not the calendar.** Let the top half of the mix dry, then soak until water drains out. In a large 10-inch or 12-inch pot, this usually means watering only once every two to three weeks in winter. Use distilled, filtered, or rainwater, or let tap water sit out overnight.
3. **Acclimate the light.** Move it out of direct south sun, since direct, hot afternoon sunlight will scorch the foliage and cause large brown burn marks. A sheer curtain or a spot a few feet back works. Step it closer over a few weeks, since it came from a dim basement.
4. **Repot in spring, one size up.** Wait until it settles. Choose a pot only slightly wider than the current one, with drainage holes and a chunky, fast-draining mix.

Trim brown tips at an angle, leaving a sliver of brown. Existing damage won't recover, but new leaves should come in clean.
